I strongly support government action to ban the sale of new petrol cars by no later than 2030. Real Hope, Real Change means facing the climate and cost-of-living crises together — and that starts with getting dirty, expensive fossil fuels off our roads. Electric vehicles are now cheaper to run and far cleaner, but people can’t make the switch alone while profits, fossil lobbies and high upfront costs stand in the way.

A 2030 ban should come with a fair transition: massive investment in public charging, free or low‑cost public transport for young people, grants and low-interest loans for battery cars where needed, and support for workers and communities affected by the shift. It must be part of a programme to insulate homes, bring energy and rail into public ownership, and introduce a wealth tax to fund the change — not let corporations profit while people pay.

This policy is about a secure future for everyone: cleaner air for our children, lower running costs for families, and a thriving green economy. For the Common Good — ban new petrol cars by 2030.

Ban the sale of new petrol cars by 2030? Absolutely oppose. This is another Net Zero diktat dreamed up in Westminster and shoved down the throats of ordinary people by the Green Blob. It’s not about cleaner air — it’s about ideology and control, and who pays the price. Working families, rural folk, and small businesses rely on reliable petrol cars: garages miles away, muddy lanes, towing trailers, shift work at odd hours. Forcing an early 2030 ban will jack up prices, wreck the used-car market, and strand people who can’t afford electric alternatives or live where charging isn’t practical.

Instead of punishing drivers, government should scrap green levies that inflate energy and motoring costs, invest in real British infrastructure — cheap home and workplace charging, better roads, and a bigger North Sea energy industry — and let consumers choose. We should stop the war on drivers and stop treating motoring as a moral failing. Scrap the 2030 petrol ban, restore common sense, and put working people before ideological gimmicks. Net Zero is Net Poverty.

I strongly support a government ban on the sale of new petrol cars by no later than 2030. This is a practical, urgent step that tackles the climate and cost-of-living crises together. Electric vehicles are cleaner and cheaper to run, but without decisive action and public investment the transition will be patchy and unfair — leaving low-income families and renters behind. A 2030 ban, paired with public ownership of energy networks, massive home and workplace charging roll-out, and a grant-backed scrappage scheme for those on low incomes, guarantees a just transition. It will speed up the shift to cheap renewable electricity, cut air pollution outside schools and hospitals, and free people from volatile petrol prices. Rather than enrich oil companies, we should ensure the benefits of cleaner transport are reinvested into our communities: better buses, safer cycle lanes, and cheaper fares for young people. Real Hope, Real Change — ban new petrol cars by 2030, for the common good and a secure future for everyone.

I strongly oppose the government’s plan to ban the sale of new petrol cars by 2030. This isn’t climate leadership — it’s a Westminster diktat that will hammer working families, rural communities and small businesses. Replacing perfectly good petrol cars with expensive electric models will leave pensioners and low‑paid workers forced into debt, while the so‑called “green” elite cheer from their London bubbles.

Electric vehicles are still unaffordable for many, have limited range in the countryside, and depend on an unreliable charging network more suitable for town commuters than farmers, tradespeople and haulage. Forcing a rapid switch will push up costs across the board — higher prices, more roadside fines, and fewer jobs in garages and the North Sea supply chain.

We should scrap ideological deadlines and focus on common‑sense solutions: expand British energy production, cut green levies from bills, and invest in practical charging infrastructure when it’s ready. No one is against better air quality, but Net Zero by diktat is Net Poverty by design. Stop the war on drivers — restore freedom, fairness and prosperity.

I strongly oppose the government’s plan to ban the sale of new petrol cars by 2030. This isn’t climate leadership — it’s a Westminster diktat that will hammer working families, rural communities and small businesses. Replacing perfectly good petrol cars with expensive electric models will leave pensioners and low‑paid workers forced into debt, while the so‑called “green” elite cheer from their London bubbles.

Electric vehicles are still unaffordable for many, have limited range in the countryside, and depend on an unreliable charging network more suitable for town commuters than farmers, tradespeople and haulage. Forcing a rapid switch will push up costs across the board — higher prices, more roadside fines, and fewer jobs in garages and the North Sea supply chain.

No one is against better air quality, but Net Zero by diktat is Net Poverty by design. Stop the war on drivers — restore freedom, fairness and prosperity.

I strongly support a government ban on the sale of new petrol cars by no later than 2030. Real Hope, Real Change means acting now to protect young people’s futures and ease the squeeze on household budgets. Electric vehicles and clean public transport are cheaper to run and far kinder to our lungs and climate than petrol cars. But a ban must be fair: we should pair it with massive investment in affordable home and street charging, retrofit grants for low-income families, and expanded free or low-cost public transport so no one is left behind.

This is about the common good — cutting emissions, lowering long-term motoring costs, and reducing air pollution outside schools and hospitals. The government should fund this transition through a wealth tax on the richest and by bringing energy and transport into public hands so profits aren’t put before people. A 2030 ban on new petrol cars, delivered alongside support for renters, workers, and rural communities, would be a bold step toward fairer, greener communities and a secure future for everyone.
